transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-05 14:00 PDT | Duration: ~64 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Luca (Redwood SE), Priya (CSM), Raj (Nimbus Platform), Sofia (ML), Daniel (Security), Terry (Networking), PM

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, can you say your names?
[00:08] Raj: Raj here, platform.
[00:10] Sofia: Sofia, ML.
[00:12] Daniel: Daniel, security.
[00:14] Terry: Terry, networking.
[00:17] Maya: Great. Luca and I will run through the Private VPC networking gotchas we saw on similar customers, then tune into runtime perf stuff — kv cache warmup, batching, quantization tradeoffs.

[02:05] Luca: Ok jumping in — the main weirdness we keep seeing is hairpin egress through corporate proxies or transitive NAT devices. Customers put Redwood Private in a VPC that must egress through their centralized proxy/NAT for compliance. With PrivateLink the control plane stays private, but inference nodes still need egress for external tokenization libraries, artifact pulls, or callouts.

[03:12] Terry: Correct, our infra team enforces egress through the proxy; we've got 2 NAT gateways in prod and HA proxies that do SSL inspection. Concern is connection tracking and sudden spikes causing conntrack table exhaustion.

[04:00] Luca: Right. Two common patterns: 1) hairpin NAT where instance source IP is translated then returns to the same subnet — this can increase latency because of extra DNAT/SNAT hops and conntrack churn; 2) using a forward proxy that breaks keep-alives and forces new TLS handshakes. Both push up p95.

[05:15] Sofia: For our SLAs we need 99th at <= 250ms for chat tokens, otherwise user experience drops. Does hairpin add 50-200ms?

[05:30] Luca: It depends. If the proxy tears down connections quickly you can see 40-120ms added per request due to TLS renegotiation + extra network hops. But batching and kv-cache change dynamics: if you have a warmed KV cache and can do batching of short requests, amortized overhead falls.

[07:00] Raj: We're worried about cost too — NAT gateway egress costs and also per-connection CPU. Any guidance to reduce NAT gateway charges?

[07:20] Maya: A couple levers: prefer PrivateLink for control-plane APIs to avoid egress; for model artifacts and model pulls you can mirror artifacts into S3 in the same account; for runtime outbound you can use VPC endpoints to internal backends where feasible to remove public egress. For unavoidable egress, consider a shared egress box (EC2+ENI) with optimized connection reuse or a L4 load balancer that preserves source IP — reduces conntrack churn vs massive NAT gateway pools.

[09:10] Terry: We also have split-horizon DNS (internal resolves different IPs). How does Redwood handle PrivateLink + split-horizon?

[09:30] Luca: Redwood Private supports split-horizon by letting you override model-hostnames to point at PrivateLink endpoints. We provide a DNS SRV note in the doc but to be explicit: if your internal DNS resolves our control plane to internal IPs, ensure resolver policy doesn't accidentally forward those through the proxy — that leads to hairpin loops. Use route table/endpoint-specific resolver rules.

[10:45] Daniel: Security — KMS integration. We want HSM-backed keys and audit logging. Any constraints if egress is via proxy?

[11:05] Maya: No constraint, but performance note: when keys are fetched for model encryption at startup, that call often adds ~200-400ms depending on KMS latency. We recommend caching DEKs locally in the runtime and rotating per policy to avoid per-request KMS hits. Also we'll supply our integration guide for AWS KMS and on-prem HSM connectors.

[12:30] Sofia: Back to runtime perf: kv-cache warmup. We've seen cold-start token regressions that kill early latency — how to pre-warm KV cache?

[13:00] Luca: Two ways: proactively replay a subset of recent prompts to the dedicated pool during ramp-up, or run a lightweight synthetic workload that exercises typical prefix lengths to populate KV. For chat workloads, you want prefix caching for common system and user starts. We'll share a small script. Note: pre-warm itself triggers egress traffic if kept external for fetches — so schedule pre-warm in same VPC region to avoid cross-regional traffic.

[14:10] Raj: How does pre-warm interact with batching settings? If you pre-warm but batch size is high, does that change latency distribution?

[14:30] Luca: Batching trades throughput for latency. A warmed KV cache reduces per-token compute, so you can afford slightly larger batches without violating p95. But if your SLO is strict (<250ms p95) we suggest dynamic batching thresholds: allow small micro-batches for tail latencies and open up to larger batches during low-latency windows. Redwood Optimize provides suggestions per workload.

[16:00] Sofia: Quantization — we are testing int8 quantized MPT variants to drop GPU memory and cost. Any impacts on compute latency jitter?

[16:20] Luca: Quantization can reduce latency per token because smaller kernels run faster, but some int8 kernels may fall back to slower paths for certain ops causing jitter. Also reduce model quality slightly; you need evals. Our runtime supports mixed-precision profiles and we can pin heavy-attention layers to fp16 while quantizing feed-forward to int8 to balance perf and quality.

[17:55] Maya: Also note kernel selection: on some GPUs (A100 vs H100) the optimal kernel differs; we choose per-device kernel at model load to reduce run-time fallback. If you plan Dedicated, we recommend telling us the instance family so we can tune the default profile.

[19:30] Terry: About conntrack — any recommendations to avoid table exhaustion?

[19:50] Luca: Tune conntrack max and timeouts on your NAT/proxy; use long-lived connections and keep-alive where possible. Alternatively, fronting Redis/broker to coalesce many small outbound requests into a single upstream call can help. Also use L4 proxies or transparent proxies that preserve established state rather than re-DNAT per flow.

[21:40] Raj: Can Redwood run entirely without any public egress? We're in a regulated environment and want zero public internet access from inference nodes.

[21:55] Maya: Yes, in private deployments we support fully air-gapped setups — model artifacts must be pushed to the local artifact store and control-plane interactions can be proxied over PrivateLink. The only caveat is when you need external tokenizers or third-party APIs — those need to be mirrored locally or proxied through your allowed egress.

[23:40] Sofia: Bandwidth consumption — at 1k rps average, what network egress should we expect for embeddings and chat?

[24:00] Luca: Depends on payload size. For chat short messages, token overhead is small but embeddings are heavier. Rough rule: 1k rps of short chat ~ 30-80Mbps depending on batch packing and streaming. Embeddings can be hundreds of Mbps. If egress costs are a concern, prefer batching + compression + VPC endpoint mirroring to avoid public egress charges.

[26:15] Terry: We use a corporate forward proxy that does TLS interception — will that break streaming responses?

[26:35] Luca: It can. Streaming uses long-lived chunked responses; if the proxy buffers or enforces content-length it can convert streaming into chunked reassembly or force buffering leading to high latency. Workaround: bypass proxy for streaming channels via route rules or use HTTP/2 multiplexing through PrivateLink if supported. We'll include recommended proxy ACLs.

[28:00] PM (Speaker 1): Quick question on tracing — can you correlate Redwood tokens to our traces? We want distributed tracing across user request -> inference runtime -> model outputs.

[28:20] Priya (CSM): We have tracing hooks: token-level cost and trace IDs are surfaced; you can inject a request ID in header and Redwood logs will include it in our console and exportable traces. We'll share the Trace API doc.

[29:45] Daniel: From security perspective, audit logs must be shipped to our SIEM; do you support syslog/S3 export?

[30:05] Maya: Yes, log export to S3/GCS and push to SIEM via Kinesis/Firehose or other connectors. For Private we can write directly to your log endpoints over PrivateLink.

[31:40] Luca: Let's do a hypothetical: you run a Dedicated pool inside your VPC, with control-plane on PrivateLink. Inbound requests from users -> ALB inside VPC -> Redwood inference nodes -> egress through corp proxy for external artifact pulls or telemetry. To avoid hairpin and conntrack you can: (a) mirror artifacts internally, (b) configure route table to reach PrivateLink without hitting NAT, and (c) use a L4 egress box for upstream TLS reuse.

[33:25] Raj: Can you share a concrete iptables/nat rule set? Our networking folks like exact examples.

[33:40] Luca: Yes — we'll share a repo snippet with iptables rules that SNAT only when destination is public and bypass for PrivateLink/internal ranges, plus conntrack tuning. That's part of the network diagram action item.

[35:10] Sofia: On the runtime side — p95 degradation when KV cache misses spike — any mitigation beyond pre-warm?

[35:30] Luca: Two mitigations: adaptive fallback to smaller model variants for tail requests (we support model variants with faster decode) and request-level QoS: mark high-priority requests to avoid batching waits. Also an LRU eviction policy tuned to your conversation horizon reduces thrash.

[37:00] Maya: Also, consider setting a second-level cache in front of the runtime (Redis) for very hot prefixes so KV cache miss penalty is reduced. But that adds operational surface.

[38:20] Terry: About IPv6 — we're moving some infra to dual-stack. Does Redwood Private support IPv6 endpoints?

[38:35] Luca: Currently control plane PrivateLink endpoints are IPv4; we have an IPv6 roadmap but for now you'll need IPv4 for runtime endpoints. If dual-stack is required we can discuss a customer-specific roadmap prioritization.

[39:50] Raj: Any quick wins to reduce p95 right now?

[40:05] Luca: Quick wins: enable KV cache warm-up on scale events, set conservative conntrack timeouts, prefer PrivateLink for control-plane, and use keep-alives on proxies. For batching: lower the latency threshold for micro-batches to reduce tail.

[41:30] Sofia: We want to test quantization profile A vs B. Can Redwood run both in the same Dedicated pool?

[41:45] Maya: We can run model variants side-by-side and route by model id. For deterministic comparison we recommend isolated runs to avoid cross-variant resource noise, but side-by-side is possible with controlled capacity pinning.

[43:10] Raj: On cost forecasting — when you say 'Dedicated pool', what's a baseline monthly cost for 2x A100 with typical utilization?

[43:30] Maya: We'll send the pricing sheet — ballpark depends on region. For a 2x A100 Dedicated committed monthly that we usually show examples for, expect a few tens of thousands per month; we'll include the egress/NAT cost examples and amortized per-token cost in the spreadsheet.

[45:00] PM: One last tricky scenario — hairpin where internal DNS returns public IP and that IP routes back through the proxy causing a loop. Any debugging tips?

[45:20] Luca: Use tcpdump at node and NAT to see TTL and SYN flow. Check resolver rules (192.168.x.x) and ensure internal resolution for Redwood hostnames points to PrivateLink IPs. Also test with curl --resolve to force the internal IP and see path.

[46:40] Daniel: About compliance — SSO, RBAC mapping to our IdP; do you support SCIM provisioning?

[46:55] Maya: Yes, SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported for Redwood Console. For Private deployments we can wire your IdP via PrivateLink and provide role mapping guidance.

[48:05] Sofia: Any gotchas about kernel settings on the inference nodes? We saw sporadic stalls likely from IRQ affinity and CPU governor.

[48:25] Luca: Set CPU governor to performance for inference nodes, pin IRQs away from GPU threads, and tune swappiness low. Also ensure NIC interrupts are balanced across cores and use hugepages for large-model memory allocations. We'll include a recommended kernel tuning doc.

[50:00] Raj: Let's recap next steps.
[50:10] Maya: Recap: Redwood action items: share hairpin NAT + iptables snippets, PrivateLink DNS guidance, KMS integration doc, quantization best-practices, and pricing + Dedicated sizing examples. Nimbus action items: provide VPC CIDR, NAT counts, sample traces from a 1k rps run, and confirm dates for a follow-up perf run.

[51:05] Terry: We'll try to run an internal test next week and share results.
[51:18] Maya: Great — shall we lock follow-up for 2026-03-12 for a perf run?
[51:25] Raj: Works for us.

[52:00] Sofia: Thanks all.
[52:10] Maya: I'll send notes and links after the call.
[52:17] Priya: I'll attach the Trace API doc and the network diagram repo link.
[52:25] Meeting end.

References mentioned: https://redwood.example.com/docs/private-vpc (doc placeholder), https://redwood.example.com/ops/kvcache-warmup-script (script placeholder), pricing-sheet link (sent after)
